title: Comparing the clinical and cost-effectiveness of colesevelam for bile acid diarrhoea with colestyramine or loperamide, including long-term follow-up
official: Comparing the clinical and cost-effectiveness of COlesevelam for Bile Acid diarrhoea with colestyramine or Loperamide, including long-Term follow-up (COBALT)
summary:
Background and study aims 
Primary bile acid diarrhoea (pBAD) is a condition that causes frequent, loose or watery bowel motions, urgency, and sometimes bowel leakage. It happens when too many bile acids reach the large bowel. pBAD affects more than 1 in 100 people in the UK, but it is often mistaken for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), which can delay diagnosis and treatment. 
Several medicines are used to treat pBAD in the NHS, including colesevelam, colestyramine and loperamide. However, there is currently not enough evidence to know which treatment works best or provides the best value for money for the NHS. 
The COBALT study aims to compare these treatments to find out which works best at improving symptoms and quality of life for people with pBAD. 

Who can participate? 
Adults aged 18 years and over who have recently been diagnosed with primary bile acid diarrhoea (pBAD) following a SeHCAT test may be able to take part. Participants must meet the study eligibility criteria and be willing to take part in study follow-up. 

What does the study involve? 
People interested in taking part will first be asked to complete a 14-day symptom and stool diary to check whether they are eligible for the study. 
Participants who are eligible will attend a hospital visit where they will provide informed consent, have some routine assessments and blood tests, and be randomly allocated by chance to receive one of three treatments:
1. Colesevelam
2. Colestyramine
3. Loperamide
Neither the participant nor their doctor can choose which treatment is allocated. 
Participants will receive treatment for 6 months. At the 6-month visit, they can choose to continue their allocated treatment for a further 6 months or switch to another treatment used for pBAD. 
Participants will be followed up for 12 months in total. They will complete symptom diaries and questionnaires about their symptoms, quality of life and daily activities. Some follow-up assessments can be completed remotely online, by telephone or on paper. Blood tests will be taken at the start of the study and again after 6 months. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
Participants may or may not experience an improvement in their symptoms. Information from this study may help improve the treatment of pBAD for future patients. 
Taking part may involve some inconvenience, including completing symptom diaries and questionnaires, attending study visits. and collecting medication from the hospital pharmacy. Blood tests may cause temporary discomfort or bruising. 
The medicines used in this study are already commonly used in NHS practice. Like all medicines, they can cause side effects. These may include constipation, bloating, abdominal discomfort, nausea, vomiting, and headaches. Participants will be monitored throughout the study, and treatment can be adjusted or stopped if needed. 

Where is the study run from? 
University of Birmingham (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
December 2026 to March 2029

Who is funding the study?
National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Health Technology Assessment Programme (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Dr Becky Case, researchgovernance@contacts.bham.ac.uk
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Has an incident diagnosis of pBAD made within the last 6 weeks based on a routine SeHCAT test with 7-day SeHCAT retention of ≤20%
2. Estimated increased stool frequency, present for the previous 6 months, defined as ≥21 stools/week (mean ≥3/day), and with ≥25% of stools being type 6/7 on the BSFS (Rome IV criteria for functional diarrhoea) assessed using a diary of daily stool frequency/type completed by participants over a 14-day period prior to randomisation (at least 7 days of data needed in order to assess eligibility)
3. Age ≥18 years
4. Willing and able to provide informed consent
5. Willing and able to be followed up as per the trial processes
Exclusion criteria:
1. Prior or current BA sequestrant treatment for pBAD
2. Other known causes of chronic diarrhoea, coeliac disease, Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) (including microscopic colitis), or exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (as outlined in national guidance)
3. Previous intestinal resection
4. Previous cholecystectomy
5. Previous biliary surgery or gastric bypass
6. Current treatment with liraglutide or any other GLP-1 receptor agonists
7. Current treatment with long-term prophylactic antibiotics
8. Current treatment with ondansetron
9. Regular opiate use (regular use of opiates is defined as taking opiates long-term on a daily basis, or on several days a week. 10. Occasional, as required use of opiates, for example using codeine to treat acute pain such as headache or joint pain, does not exclude participation)
11. Any other medical disorder that in the opinion of the investigator would prohibit trial-related procedures
12. Any other medication use that is contraindicated alongside the study medication
13. Current participation in another Clinical Trial of an Investigational Product (CTIMP)
14. Known to be pregnant, actively trying to get pregnant or breastfeeding (Patients can be re-screened to confirm their eligibility, immediately after breastfeeding has completed) 
15. Not willing to use effective contraception to prevent pregnancy (where appropriate)
